source.title: Understanding Video Transformers via Universal Concept Discovery
source.authors: M. Kowal; Achal Dave; Rares Ambrus; Adrien Gaidon; K. Derpanis; P. Tokmakov

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies concept discovery in video-transformer representations, not neuron-pole explanations or the claim versions. It notes that neurons do not capture the full extent of distributed representations, but does not test the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites work on shared neurons and says neurons cannot explain the full extent of distributed representations. Its experiments concern spatiotemporal concepts in video models, not neuron poles, language models, activation-based explanation tests, or attribution graphs.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes VTCD, a concept-discovery method that clusters attention-head key features in video transformers. It never measures individual neuron interpretability shares, tests explanations of neurons, or builds neuron attribution graphs. Its only neuron-related content is one sentence in related work: neurons cannot explain the full extent of distributed representations. That is an unsupported assertion citing Toy Models of Superposition, not a result. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses', since there is no substantive engagement with the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. VTCD extracts human-interpretable, importance-ranked concepts from video transformers. Shared concepts across models reveal common processing: a spatiotemporal basis early and object-tracking representations later. Head pruning and VOS applications are also shown.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates VTCD, a method for discovering distributed spatiotemporal concepts in video-transformer representations; it does not reproduce the cited neuron-explanation methods.
record.method_sensitivity: No outcome sensitivity test is reported; SLIC compactness is tuned separately for each model.

fits_no_version.finding: VTCD found 40 Rosetta 4-concept tuples shared across four video transformers trained on different objectives. Their mean R-score was 17.1, against 0.6 for all 4-concepts (Sec. 5.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Video transformers trained on different objectives share distributed spatiotemporal concepts, such as early positional bases and mid-layer object tracking.

record.problems: The evidence concerns video-vision representations rather than language-model neurons. The shared-concept analysis is reported for four models and is not a test of neuron-level explanation fidelity.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's action-classification head-pruning and DAVIS'16 video-object-segmentation results are omitted because they do not measure neuron interpretability or any listed claim version (Sections 5.1 and 5.3; Tables 2 and 3).

record.verdict_notes: The neuron remark is a related-work assertion with no supporting experiment, so it should not be treated as evidence on V1, V4 or V6. The paper works with head-level clustered features, not neurons.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole shares and explanation tests on held-out activations.
Neuron-pole shares across language models, dense or MoE architectures, and scale.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose interpretation, and recursive generalization.
Neuron interpretability shares across architectures, regularization, tools, and vision-model scale.
Attribution graphs using a large model’s own neurons and comparison with trained replacement models.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire on new inputs.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.measure: Number and mean R-score of Rosetta 4-concept tuples; comparison with the mean R-score among all possible 4-concepts
rows.note: The result concerns shared distributed concepts in video-transformer representations; it does not measure neuron interpretability shares or any of the listed claim versions.
rows.check: Measures concept-support overlap (Rosetta concepts) across four video transformers, not neuron interpretability, so it bears on no version. The reported 'average R-score 17.1' versus 0.6 is likely in percent mIoU; the units are unstated in the paper. This is the study's own method output, not a claim test.

relation.reason: Its only neuron content is two passing related-work remarks (Rosetta Neurons [19], 3D-CNN neuron visualisation [22]): neurons cannot capture distributed representations. That is a mention, not a test. 'discusses' would also be defensible. Note that this 2024 paper predates and does not cite the original essay.

tranche.reason: The paper proposes VTCD (concept discovery over attention-head features in video transformers). It never measures neuron interpretability shares, explanations or neuron circuits, and it neither tests nor uses the claim.

source_check.notes: Bears on no claim version. Rosetta R-scores are support-mask IoU and seem to be on a percent scale (17.1 vs 0.6), but the text gives no unit. Its only neuron-related content is a related-work assertion that neurons cannot explain distributed representations, with no measurement behind it.
